questions.prompt: You run one session with `--worktree`, then spawn three subagents that each rewrite a different file — but two of them import the same shared helper and both rewrite it. Nothing errors, and at the end there is no conflict to resolve. What actually happened?
options: The session worktree isolated the subagents from each other, so their edits landed on separate branches
Claude Code refused the overlapping edits but reported success anyway
All three subagents shared the session's one worktree, so the second writer overwrote the first in the same file
The two subagents each got a temporary worktree, which is why there was no conflict
questions.explanation: A session worktree gives the whole session one checkout; subagents without `isolation: worktree` inherit it. Two writers, one file, second wins. Option D is the tempting wrong answer because it sounds like a feature — but per-agent worktrees only appear when a subagent's frontmatter asks for them, and then a conflict would be possible rather than absent. The absence of any conflict is the clue that there was only one copy.

questions.prompt: You want three subagents to refactor three separate packages in parallel without any chance of them touching each other's files. You are not currently in a worktree session. What is the smallest change that gives you that?
options: Add `isolation: worktree` to the frontmatter of the subagent they share
Run each subagent with a different model
questions.explanation: Per-agent isolation is the scope that stops agents colliding with each other; `isolation: worktree` in the subagent's frontmatter gives each run its own checkout. Option B is the tempting wrong answer because `--worktree` is the command you know, but it isolates the session from other sessions and leaves the three agents sharing one folder. Models and `.gitignore` change nothing about who edits which folder.

questions.prompt: A subagent is configured with `isolation: worktree` and must build on a commit you made but have not pushed. By default its worktree branches from the default branch, so it does not see your commit. What do you change?
options: Add the commit hash to the subagent's `description` field
Check out the branch in the main folder before running the subagent
Nothing — an isolated worktree always carries your unpushed commits
questions.explanation: `worktree.baseRef` controls the base: `"fresh"` (the default) branches from the default branch, `"head"` branches from your current local HEAD, including unpushed commits. Option C is the tempting wrong answer because it reverses the default. Option B does not help — an isolated worktree is a separate checkout and does not follow the main folder's current branch.

questions.prompt: Two subagents only read code and return a written analysis; they never edit files. A colleague insists you must give them `isolation: worktree` or they will collide. Are they right?
options: Yes — any two subagents that run at once need separate worktrees
No — read-only agents cannot collide on files, so isolation buys nothing and costs a checkout each
Yes, because the second subagent's context window overwrites the first
No, because `isolation: worktree` is not valid on a subagent
questions.explanation: Isolation protects files from concurrent writes. Agents that do not write files have nothing to collide on, so per-agent worktrees add setup cost for no safety. Option A is the tempting wrong answer because it turns a real rule ('parallel writers need isolation') into a blanket one. Option D is simply false — `isolation: worktree` is valid subagent frontmatter.
